question: A report prepared for the European Commission suggests that the EU has just one or two years to take effective action before its ability to close the gap in the development of cuttingedge AI is further diminished. Europe accounts for only around 5 % of global computing power, whilst US companies dominate in the development of frontier AI models and in access to the infrastructure necessary for training them.

At the same time, European companies are grappling with high energy prices, limited access to capital, protracted investment procedures and growing regulatory obligations. The Commission is today being warned by its own experts of the risk of Europe becoming permanently dependent on non-European suppliers of the most advanced AI systems. In this connection: 1.

How does the Commission assess its AI policy to date, and does it recognise that the insufficient prioritisation of computing power, energy, investment and business scaling – whilst focusing on new regulatory obligations – has contributed to Europe’s current lag behind the global leaders?
What specific barriers to investment in computing power, data centres and the development of the most advanced AI models does the Commission intend to remove over the next two years?

Will the Commission reassess existing and planned regulatory burdens relating to AI where these may further limit the ability of European businesses to scale up their operations and compete on the global market?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (24.9.2026) At the start of the mandate, the Commission set the objective of making the EU an AI Continent. This translated into policy attention on a number of key dimensions: computing infrastructures, high-quality data, AI adoption, talent and skills, and regulatory simplification.

This has led, among others, to the launch of several initiatives including the Apply AI Strategy1, aimed at supporting the integration of AI in strategic sectors and strengthening competitiveness of European businesses.

Building on the AI Continent Action Plan2, the Commission proposed the AI Omnibus3 and supported its negotiations by the co-legislators, which introduced targeted simplifications to lower the compliance burden for companies.

The Commission also launched its most ambitious initiative to date to expand the EU’s AI computing capacity: a call for tenders to establish AI Gigafactories4 in the EU, which is expected to mobilise at least EUR 30 billion in public and private investment. More broadly, the EU needs to reinforce its capacity across the entire AI stack. This is the goal of the recent Tech Sovereignty Package5.

Among others, the Cloud and AI Development Act6 aims to encourage investment in computing capacity by addressing existing barriers, while also supporting the development of frontier, physical and industrial AI.

Furthermore, the Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the energy sector7 introduced a strategic initiative where EU grid operators and solutions providers are developing sovereign AI models for planning and managing electricity grids.
At the same time, maintaining Europe’s competitiveness in this field will require sustained efforts and investment from all actors in the EU, notably its leading industrial companies.
